nameStory: The name 'spindle' comes from the plant's traditional use in making spindles for spinning thread — the hard, dense wood was perfect for this delicate work. European craftsmen prized spindle wood for centuries, shaping it into tools for textile work and even into skewers and knitting needles.
description: Spindle is a deciduous shrub or small tree that typically grows 6-20 feet tall, with an upright, somewhat open branching pattern. This European native has escaped cultivation in parts of New England, where it's sometimes found growing wild. It's most famous for its eye-catching fall display of bright pink fruits that split open to reveal orange seeds, creating a stunning two-toned color combination that's hard to miss.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Four-lobed pink capsules about the size of a marble that split open in fall to reveal bright orange seeds dangling on thin threads — this shocking pink and orange combination is unmistakable

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Simple, oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stems, with finely toothed edges and a smooth texture that feels slightly waxy to the touch

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are distinctly green and four-angled or slightly square in cross-section, while older bark becomes grayish-brown and develops shallow furrows

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, inconspicuous greenish-white flowers with four petals that appear in late spring, easily overlooked but worth noting for their subtle sweet scent

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms an upright shrub or small tree with somewhat sparse branching, often wider at the top than the base, giving it an open, airy appearance

habitat: In New England, spindle is most often found as an escaped ornamental near old homesteads, along woodland edges, and in hedgerows. It prefers well-drained, fertile soils and thrives in areas with some lime content, often establishing in disturbed sites where it can get partial to full sun.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in late April to May, followed by small clusters of greenish-white flowers that are easy to miss but have a faint sweet fragrance.
seasonality.summer: The plant is fairly unremarkable in summer, with its simple green foliage blending into the background until you notice the developing green fruits.
seasonality.fall: This is showtime — the spectacular pink fruits split open to reveal dangling orange seeds, while leaves may turn pale yellow before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the angular green stems and any persistent fruits, while the overall sparse branching pattern becomes most obvious.

funFact: The bright orange seeds don't just look like tiny Halloween decorations — they're actually covered in a fatty coating called an aril that birds love to eat, which is why you'll often find new spindle plants growing under bird perches and power lines where the seeds get deposited.
confusionNotes: The distinctive pink and orange fruit display is so unique that spindle is rarely confused with anything else when in fruit, but without fruits it might be mistaken for other opposite-leaved shrubs — just remember to look for those characteristic square green stems.
contextualKnowledge: While called 'European spindle,' this plant has been cultivated in North America for so long that many people assume it's native — it's actually an introduced species that has naturalized in some areas, though it's not considered aggressively invasive like some of its relatives.
compareHints: Unlike its notorious relative winged euonymus (burning bush), European spindle lacks the prominent corky 'wings' on its stems and has much less intense fall leaf color. Fortune's spindle is typically a low-growing groundcover, while wahoo is our native spindle with purple (not pink) fruits and is much rarer in New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Euonymus relatives in New England, winged euonymus is the only one with prominent corky wings on the stems.
Unlike winged euonymus (burning bush) which is deciduous with prominent corky wing-like ridges on stems, Fortune's spindle stays evergreen and has smooth, round stems.
American wahoo differs from its cousin winged euonymus (burning bush) by lacking the distinctive corky wings on its stems and being much less common.
Among New England's euonymus species, Hamilton's spindle stands out for its four-lobed pink fruits and dangling orange seeds on threads.

Large-leaved spindle stands out from its New England relatives primarily by leaf size – its leaves are significantly larger than the small leaves of winged euonymus or the narrow leaves of other spindle species.
Unlike its deciduous relatives like winged euonymus (burning bush) or wahoo, Japanese spindle keeps its leaves year-round.
